content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Night symbolizes spiritual darkness—sin, evil, unbelief, and separation from God—as the counterpart of day/light (God, Christ, truth). A common secondary reading treats night eschatologically as the present evil age awaiting the dawn of Christ's return; other strands (trial, death/lost opportunity, prayerful encounter, literal time marker) are acknowledged as secondary.","book_summary":"Night is the absence of Day and Light, which the book defines specifically as 'visible obedience'; it is marked by sleep or death and by sinful deeds concealed in darkness. At the largest scale it is the fixed historical era from the fall of man until the Kingdom of God begins on earth. Opposite: Day.","consensus_core_identification":"Night = the condition/realm of spiritual darkness (sin, evil, unbelief, separation from God), contrasted with day/light; secondarily the present evil age before Christ's return.","book_core_identification":"Night = absence of visible obedience (the book's technical definition of Day/Light), characterized by sleep, death, and concealed sin; macro-scale: the epoch from the fall until the earthly Kingdom of God.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book tightens the consensus's broad 'spiritual darkness/sin' into a specific technical antithesis: absence of 'visible obedience' rather than generic evil or unbelief. It also fixes the eschatological reading to a definite span—from the fall of man until the Kingdom begins on earth—whereas the consensus's eschatological alternative treats night as the present age before Christ's return without anchoring its start at the fall. The book folds sleep and death into the definition as marks of night, whereas the consensus lists death/sleep as separate minority applications; and it drops the consensus's acknowledgments of positive night uses (prayer, revelation, rest) and purely literal uses.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book's central referent remains within the consensus category: night as the negative counterpart of day/light, associated with sin done in darkness and with the age preceding God's kingdom—both attested in the consensus (primary meaning plus the common eschatological alternative). However, the book materially changes precision and boundaries: (1) it redefines the contrast term as 'visible obedience,' a narrower and more specific identification than generic divine light/truth; (2) it dates the macro 'night' from the fall rather than from an unspecified point in the present age; (3) it integrates sleep and death as constitutive marks rather than separate senses; (4) it implicitly excludes the positive/neutral senses (night prayer, rest, revelation, literal usage) that the consensus admits. This is real boundary and extension disagreement without replacement of the core referent, so REFINED rather than MATCH or DIVERGENT.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for MATCH: the book's entry is essentially the standard darkness/sin reading plus the well-known eschatological 'present age' reading, and 'visible obedience' is merely the book's cross-referenced gloss of Light rather than a substantive change to what Night itself denotes. On this view the differences are wording and compression, not boundary disagreement.","confidence":"medium"}
